title: Chapter 200 – Hua's Page
html:
[Bell's Surgery and the Roll Room – Hua]

Hua has learned to sit still in a room where someone is dying.

It is a skill she did not know she had. It came to her on the second night, in Bell's narrow surgery with its camphor and warm wax, while the healer worked and the child on the cot fought for her breath. The others fidgeted. Tian Mo paced. Qinghe fed the fire and fed it again. But Hua sat on a stool in the corner with her hands folded in her lap, and her body knew exactly what to do: be quiet, be useful, be there. She does not remember learning it. Her hands remember. They know where the basin stands without looking, and how a cloth must be wrung, and the angle at which one tips a cup to a mouth that cannot swallow.

I was a healer, she thinks, watching Bell's small back. Before I was a Warden. Before I was anything.

"Hot water," says Bell.

Hua is already on her feet. She brings it, steaming, in the copper basin, and sets it on the table without a drop spilled. Bell glances at her, sharp and quick, and says nothing. But there is something in the glance, a kind of dry recognition, and Hua feels it all the way down her spine.

On the cot, Little Mei lies under three quilts with her brown hair stuck to her forehead. Her face is the color of tallow. Her breath comes in short uneven catches, like a clock that has lost its beat, and every few minutes her whole body jolts, a hard little spasm that arches her back off the pillow. Tian Mo kneels at the bedside with his stone hand spread across her ribs. A faint green light pulses under his fingers. He has not moved in three hours. He has not spoken in four.

"The root-light slows it," says Bell, low, to no one. "It does not stop it. It's a candle against a flood."

"How long?" asks Jian.

He stands in the doorway, as he has stood most of the night, leaning on his staff. Mei is beside him, a thin faint shimmer, one hand pressed to her mouth. Neither has sat down.

"Hours. A day, perhaps." Bell does not turn. "I have never seen it in one so small. The Seven had it as babies, and it was mild. They grew into it. This is... faster. It is as if the body were making up for lost time."

"Lost time," repeats Mei, very quietly.

"She was held in the Bloom for six hundred years. The fault was waiting." Bell wrings the cloth. "It has been waiting for the first warm breath."

Nobody answers. The fire cracks. In the cot, the child makes a small thin sound, and Hua, without knowing she has moved, is on her knees beside the bed with the child's hot hand in hers.

* * *

Near the end of the night Jian sits down beside her.

He does it clumsily, as he does everything now, lowering himself onto the next stool with a hand on the wall and a controlled grunt. He smells of camphor and old ink. His face in the firelight is all bones. For a time he says nothing, and she lets him, watching the thin chest of the child on the cot rise and fall.

"You were a healer," he says at last.

"How do you know?"

"You hold a cup differently from the rest of us." A faint smile. "And you have not once panicked."

"I may be panicking quietly."

"That is also a healer's skill." He turns his head. "I wanted to ask you something. It is not a good time. I am sorry."

"Ask."

"The mark on your hand. It opened the door to ARK-6. It glows when you are afraid. Does it do anything else?"

She looks at her palm. The pale ring, the gap, the nine spokes. "I do not know."

"May I?"

She holds it out. He does not touch it. He only looks, and she sees his eyes lose focus, the way a man's do when he reads a letter held very close. A silver line runs from the corner of his left eye to his jaw, and she notices it for the first time, thin as a hair, beautiful and terrible.

"It is a key," he says slowly. "Not only to the Annex. To the Roll, I think. To the whole archive of the Hall. The Interface says..." He stops. "It says that what you do not remember is not lost. It is merely unread."

"Then why can't I read it?"

"Because the Warden locked it." He lowers his gaze. "Six hundred years ago, on purpose. And the lock is you."

She is silent. The child on the cot gives a thin cry, and Tian Mo's hand tightens.

"If I opened it," says Hua. "What would it cost?"

"I do not know." He hesitates. "I would not ask. Except that I think the answer to this..." He looks at the child, and his voice fails. "I think it is in there."

She meets his eyes for a long moment. They are dark and exhausted and unafraid.

"Ask me again at dawn," she says.

At dawn Mo Yan comes in, and Hua nearly does not look up.

She hears the soft step on the boards, the creak of a shoe. She knows it for her daughter's before she sees. It is a strange knowing, to be certain of a person you do not remember. It lives in her ears, in the back of her neck. A small hand slips into hers, warm and a little sticky with sleep, and Hua closes her fingers round it and holds it.

Mo Yan does not speak. She leans against her mother's shoulder and looks at the cot.

"She will be all right," says Hua. She does not know that she believes it.

The girl shakes her head. It is a small slow motion, grave as a judge's. She lifts her free hand, flat, and then taps two fingers to her temple and draws them down her cheek in a slow curve, like a tear. Sad. Then she points at Hua.

"Me?"

A firm nod.

"I'm not sad," says Hua. "I'm tired."

The girl's gray eyes do not waver. She raises both hands and makes a shape in the air: a small box, a lid, a hand turning a key. Then she puts her palm flat on her mother's chest, over the heart, and presses.

You have something locked. Open it.

Hua stares at her. The fire hums. Somewhere in the walls a pipe knocks. She feels the little palm like a stone on her breastbone, and the mark on her own hand, the pale ring with its gap and nine small spokes, begins very faintly to glow.

"I can't," she whispers.

Mo Yan's brows draw together.

"Not yet. It might..." Hua swallows. "It might cost something. I don't know what. I might lose..."

She does not finish. She does not have to. The girl's face changes, softens, and she throws her arms round her mother's neck and holds on. It is a fierce, clumsy, wordless embrace, and Hua feels the small body shaking against hers.

I know, it says. I know you might. Do it anyway.

"Why?"

The girl pulls back. She lifts her hands and speaks, slowly, with the grave precision of a child who has rehearsed a thing many times. Her fingers shape the signs, and Hua, who has not been taught them, understands every word.

You were the Warden. You kept the sleepers. You chose the eight. You knew the sickness. If anyone knows how to stop it, it is you.

Hua looks at the cot. At the thin white face. At Tian Mo's stone hand pulsing green on the narrow ribs.

"Show me the Roll Room," she says.

* * *

The room is empty at this hour, and the light is gray.

It falls through the high window in a pale slab and lies across the brick floor, and the dust that turns in it is slow and heavy. The shelves climb into shadow. The air smells of old paper and cold ink. In the middle of the long desk sits the lacquer box, open, and in it the Stillborn Roll with its narrow black spines.

Hua stops in the door.

She has been here before. Not in this body, not in this year, but she has been here. She knows the creak of the third board from the left. She knows that the oil lamp on the desk will not light unless the wick is trimmed. She knows, without being told, that the window has never been opened and that the sill is carved with nine small circles that nobody has noticed in six centuries.

"Go on," says Zhao, from the desk.

She starts. She had not seen him. He is sitting in the corner with a blanket over his knees and a pen in his hand, and he has the gray, sleepless look of a man who has been there all night. He does not smile. He pushes back his stool and rises.

"I will leave you," he says. "If you wish. I have kept the room for forty years. I would not be sorry to be elsewhere."

"Stay."

"Are you certain?"

"I am not certain of anything." She sets her hand on the lid of the lacquer box. It is cool and smooth, worn pale where a thumb has rested. Her thumb. She knows it by the fit. "But I would rather not be alone."

He sits down again, slowly. He says nothing more.

She lifts the Roll. She turns to the first page of the oldest ledger, the one that begins in the Year 3, and lays her bare palm flat on the brown paper. The ring-shaped mark glows, a faint steady ember. The ink beneath her hand seems to darken.

Open, she thinks, to nothing, to the dark.

Nothing happens. She holds her breath. Zhao's pen scratches in the corner, stops. A long moment passes, and another, and she is on the point of drawing back when the paper warms under her palm, and the room tilts.

* * *

It is raining on the day the ring is raised.

She stands in a vast raw cavern of black rock, under a ceiling not yet vaulted, with her gown sodden to the knee. A hundred workers crowd the floor. A hundred more hang from rope scaffolds against the walls. Everywhere is the shriek of iron, the hiss of silver being poured into channels, the bright wild glare of the Gate's old fire. At the center of it all, under a tarp, sits a thing like a huge round table, and beside it stand nine men and women in the plain gray of the Founders.

She knows them. She has known them for years. There is the tall one with the ruined hands, who cannot stop apologizing. There is the broad dark woman with the scar through her lip who has not slept since the Seam opened. There is the Cartographer, the Ferryman, and the old man Brenn who cannot hold a cup. There is Ma Ruo-lin, sharp and small and fierce, with ink to her elbows and a stylus behind her ear. And there is Ethan, thinner than any of them, who looks at Hua across the cavern with the eyes of a man who has not slept in a month and has decided to be kind.

"You're late," he says.

"I was with the medics."

"And?"

"They want to go in first." She comes forward, shaking the rain from her cloak. "All ten. Ring One. They've agreed. They think it's better if the first sleepers are the ones who can read the threads."

"Ten," says Ma Ruo-lin. "I count nine."

"There is one who will not be named."

A silence falls. The Cartographer, a heavy man with a stoop, rubs his eyes. The Ferryman looks at his boots. Ethan alone meets her gaze.

"The Tenth," he says.

"The Tenth." She sets her jaw. "He says he'll hold the top of the stair. He says someone must go up, or the Seam will find the way round. He says he's willing."

"He's not willing." Ma Ruo-lin's voice cracks like a whip. "He's afraid, and he's proud, and he thinks the rest of us are fools."

"He may be right."

"He may be a great many things. He will still be alone."

"So will we all," says Ethan softly. "Eventually."

She does not answer. The rain drums on the tarp. Beyond it, in the dark, she hears the roar of the Bloom, far away and patient, like a tide that has not yet found the shore.

"The medics," she says. "Ring One. They carry the remedy."

"The Quiet Remedy."

"Yes."

"They know the cost?"

"All of it." She looks at the round table. At the empty beds that will ring it, row on row,, lined with silver, waiting. "They are the ones who built it. They are the only ones who can keep it. If a child of the line falls sick with the fault, they will wake. They will be needed. They will be the last of the old world's medicine. And when they die, the remedy dies with them."

"There is a second copy," says Ma Ruo-lin. She is not looking at anyone. She is looking at the stylus in her hand, and her voice has gone very flat. "There must be. A remedy that lives in four hundred bodies is a remedy that dies when they do. It needs a second home."

"A living one," says the Cartographer.

"A young one." Ma Ruo-lin's jaw tightens. "A child of the valley's line, born with the fault. It will carry the remedy as a seed carries a tree. It will not know. It will grow up and be well, and if the day ever comes that the medics are gone..."

"You are asking us to put a medicine in a baby."

"I am asking us to put a promise in one."

Ethan does not speak. Hua sees his hands, thin and shaking on the edge of the table. She sees him look at the ruined hands of the tall man beside him and then at his own.

"How many?" he says at last.

"Enough to be safe," says Hua. Her own voice sounds far away. "Eight."

"Why eight?"

"Because nine is the Nine," she says, "and I will not ask a child to be one of us."

Ma Ruo-lin nods once, sharply, and writes something down. The stylus scratches loud in the sudden quiet.

"Then it is decided," she says. "Eight children. Heaven help us all, it is decided."

"Heaven help us," says Hua, and closes her eyes. "And them."

* * *

She comes back with a gasp.

The room is gray. Her face is wet. Zhao is on his feet, a few steps away, with one hand outstretched as though to catch her, and his eyes are enormous.

"What did you see?" he says.

"The ring." Her voice is a thread. "The raising of it. The Founders. The ten medics..." She presses her hand to her mouth. "Ring One. The lamps that went out. Zhao, the lamps that went out in the Hall, the first ones, the oldest..."

"Four hundred and twelve," says Zhao. "And sixty-one."

"Four hundred and seventy-three." She is trembling. "They were not just sleepers. They were the remedy. They were the cure for the blood fault. The Founders' medics, the last of them, put to sleep in the first ring to wait for a child who would need them."

"And they are gone."

"They are gone." The words fall like stones. "Ethan's walk. The bridge, the tree. Every time he went through Door Six, it took them. The oldest lamps are the ones the ring draws on first. It drew them dry."

Zhao has gone the color of ash. "Then the child..."

"The remedy is dead," says Hua.

She sits down on the floor. She does not decide to. Her knees fold. She sits in the middle of the Roll Room with her back against the lacquer box and the ledger in her lap and stares at the white wall. She thinks of a girl in a cot, small and burning. She thinks of a boy who coughs blood, and a ghost who walked into the snow to see a tree, and four hundred and seventy-three lamps going out one by one like candles in a draft.

Nobody did it on purpose. That is the cruelty. A father walked to see his wife. A ring did what rings do. A door took what it was built to take. And somewhere under the earth, for six hundred years, a whole medicine waited patiently for the one child who would need it, and died the week she woke.

She is aware of a small warm hand on her shoulder. Mo Yan has come in. She kneels on the brick floor and puts her arms round her mother's neck, and Hua leans into her without a word.

"I am so sorry," she whispers. "I kept them. I kept them so long. And I let them go."

* * *

She sits with the ledger until her legs go numb, and Zhao brings her tea she cannot drink.

He moves around the Roll Room with the soft shuffling tread of an old man, putting things back where they belong. He closes the lacquer box. He straightens the scrolls. He does not look at her, and she is grateful. When he finally sits, it is on the lowest rung of the stepladder, a thin gray man with ink on three fingers and a cup in his lap.

"I knew a boy once," he says. "Forty years ago. He had the tremor."

"Did he die?"

"No. He grew up. He became a very good carpenter. He built half the benches in the clan hall." Zhao stares into his tea. "The ledger said born still. But he was not. His mother hid him in the cellar for three nights, and my father, who was Steward before me, wrote it in black anyway. It is the only lie I ever knew him tell."

"Why?"

"Because the Warden of the Hall came to take stillborn children, and my father could not bear the thought."

She goes quite cold. "He knew."

"He knew something. Not all." Zhao lifts his eyes. "He said that the Hall took children who did not live, and that the clan should be grateful, and that in forty years he had never once seen one come back. He wrote that on the last page of his book. I do not like it. That is all."

"He was right not to."

"Was he?" The old man's voice is gentle. "I have been thinking, Warden. All night. About the eight. About what you did, or what the woman you were did. And I find..." He hesitates. "I find I cannot hate her."

"Why not?"

"Because she wrote I do not know whether I have done right. In the margin. In her own hand. A person who writes that has not yet stopped being a person." He sets down the cup. "My father wrote almost the same words. Perhaps it is a Lin thing. Perhaps it is a human one."

Hua closes her eyes. She cannot speak.

The price of the memory arrives quietly, an hour later.

She does not notice it at first. She is in the corridor outside the surgery, with Mo Yan's hand in hers, walking back to the cot where the child lies breathing in short gasps. She is thinking about the medics, the stair, the Tenth. She is thinking of a great many things she has not thought of for six centuries. And then, at the door, she looks down at the small girl beside her and a strange, cold, empty feeling goes through her like a hand through water.

She stares at the child.

A thin pale face. A brown braid, half undone. Gray eyes, a little too wide. A fierce set to the chin that she should know, that she has watched for seven days, that she has known in the dark by its step alone.

"Who are you?" says Hua.

Mo Yan's hand tightens on hers.

"I'm sorry." Her voice is thin and strange. "I'm so sorry. I... You're holding my hand. You've been here all night. I know your name, I know it, it's—"

The words are gone. She searches for them. She reaches into the place where a week of love should be and there is nothing there at all. A page, torn out. A clean white margin.

"The Roll," she says. "It took something. It took the week."

Mo Yan's face does not change. She does not weep. She only studies her mother, with her head a little on one side, as a doctor studies a patient. Then she does something Hua has not seen her do. She reaches up, slowly, and tucks a lock of hair behind her left ear.

Hua stares. The motion is small and shy and entirely familiar. She tucks her hair behind the left ear when she is about to say something she thinks is foolish. The sentence rises in her mind from nowhere, in her own voice, a week old, and the white margin trembles.

And then she does not say it.

She falls to her knees. The child's arms are round her before she touches the floor. She hears herself saying the name, over and over, Mo Yan, Mo Yan, Mo Yan, and every time the name comes back a little more, as water comes back into a dry well, until at last she is weeping into the small shoulder and the child is stroking her hair.

"It came back," she says. "It came back. I didn't lose you."

Not all, signs Mo Yan, over her mother's shoulder. A little. I'll tell you again.

"Tell me everything."

Everything, signs the girl.

"Hua."

The voice is dry and hoarse, and it comes from the end of the corridor. She lifts her head.

A man stands there in a gray gown, with a blanket over his shoulders and a cup in his hand. He is lean and dark and shaven-headed. His black eyes are bright and fixed. He has been standing perfectly still for some time, she thinks; he has the stillness of one who has heard a good deal.

"Warden," says Perrin Ado. "I have been looking for you."

She gets to her feet. She is shaky, but she is standing. "You're the Archivist."

"Third Division. Yes." He inclines his head, a short stiff bow. "I was told you had opened the Roll. I came to see whether it had told you the rest."

"The rest?"

"The index." His mouth twists. "Four hundred and seventy-three medics are gone. I keep the notes they left. I was put to sleep with the archive, and I woke with it in my head, and I have been trying for two days to find someone I could say it to."

"Say what?"

"That the remedy was never only theirs." His black eyes burn. "It was copied. Once. A single time. Into a living vessel. A child of the line, born in the valley and kept whole." He swallows. "The Warden chose eight. You told them it was for safekeeping. It was not."

Hua's heart stops.

"The Seven carry the remedy," says Perrin Ado. "And the eighth. And the ninth. They are the cure. Every one of them. And the only way to give it to the girl on that cot is to take it from them."
